courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Why radiance fields needed a rasterizer instead of ray marching
question: A colleague says 3DGS is fast because it uses a smaller neural network than NeRF. What is the more accurate explanation?
options: It uses a hash grid to make the MLP queries cheaper, like InstantNGP
It renders at lower resolution and upsamples the result
It has no network at render time: explicit Gaussians are projected and alpha blended by a sorting rasterizer
It skips the transmittance term, so each sample is independent
explain: 3DGS has no neural network at all. The scene is a list of Gaussians with stored parameters, and rendering is projection plus sorted alpha blending. The blending formula still includes transmittance; it is the same image formation model as NeRF.

courseTitle: 3D Gaussian splatting: real-time radiance fields from photos
lessonTitle: Memory cost, ablations, failure modes and gsplat in practice
question: Compared with Mip-NeRF360, which statement about 3DGS (30K iterations) on the Mip-NeRF360 dataset matches the paper?
options: Higher PSNR, faster training, and a smaller model
Slightly lower PSNR, much faster training and rendering, and a much larger model
Same PSNR and same model size, but faster rendering
Lower quality on every metric, but real-time rendering
explain: Table 1: PSNR 27.21 vs 27.69 dB (slightly lower), but SSIM and LPIPS slightly better, training about 42 minutes vs 48 hours, 134 vs 0.06 FPS, and 734 MB vs 8.6 MB.

courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Hazard pointers and epochs: stop reuse while anyone looks
question: In the hazard pointer pop, a developer removes the line that re-checks top.load() != t after announcing t. What can go wrong?
options: Nothing, the announcement alone protects t
The CAS will always fail
Between reading t and announcing it, t may have been popped, retired and freed by a scan that did not see the announcement, so reading t->next touches freed memory
explain: Michael's condition requires the hazard pointer to cover the node from a time when it was still reachable. The re-check proves t was still on the stack after the announcement was visible, so any later scan must see it. Without it, a retire and scan can slip in before the announcement.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Who are you, and what may you do: authentication vs authorization
question: A support ticket API checks that a valid session cookie is present, then returns `/tickets/:id` for any id. Which principle does this break?
options: Open design
Complete mediation: the access to this specific ticket is never checked for authority
Psychological acceptability
Nothing: the cookie check is the authorization
explain: The cookie check is authentication. Complete mediation says every access to every object must be checked: the server must ask whether this user may read this ticket, not only whether some user is logged in.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Sequential vs random ids, and why random ids are not authorization
question: A team replaces sequential order ids with UUIDv4 and removes the ownership check, reasoning that nobody can guess a UUID. Which statement is correct?
options: This is safe because RFC 9562 guarantees UUIDs are unguessable
This is unsafe because ids leak through links, logs and other responses, and RFC 9562 says UUIDs must not be used as security capabilities
This is unsafe because UUIDv4 is predictable from timestamps
This is safe as long as the ids are sent in POST bodies
explain: Guessing is no longer practical, but possession of a leaked id would open the object. RFC 9562 explicitly forbids using UUIDs as identifiers whose mere possession grants access. Keep the ownership check.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Cases: USPS, Peloton and Optus, APIs that trusted too much
question: Peloton's first fix made an endpoint require login. Why did Pen Test Partners still call it unfixed?
options: Because the login page itself was vulnerable
Because anyone can create an account, so the same private data still went to any authenticated user
Because GraphQL cannot be secured
Because the endpoint used POST instead of GET
explain: The data exposure was an authorization problem: the API never checked whether the requester may see this rider's details. Requiring authentication only changed the audience from everyone to everyone with a free account.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Testing authorization with role matrices, and detecting enumeration
question: An enumeration alert keyed only on source IP never fires, even though one account downloaded 200,000 records. What is the most likely reason?
options: The account used HTTPS
Denials were logged as 404s
The records were returned as JSON
Requests were spread across many IP addresses, so no single IP crossed the threshold; counters should also be keyed by account or token
explain: Spreading requests over many addresses defeats per-IP counting, which is what Optus said its attacker did. Count distinct objects and denials per account, session or API key as well.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: NTLM relay: forwarding someone else's login, and how signing stops it
question: Which control is Microsoft's primary mitigation for PetitPotam-style relay to AD CS web enrollment?
options: Disable Kerberos on the CA
Add the CA to Protected Users
Rotate the krbtgt password
Enable EPA and require HTTPS on the enrollment services
explain: KB5005413 recommends enabling Extended Protection for Authentication and disabling HTTP on the AD CS web enrollment services, so a relayed login fails the channel binding check.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Delegation: letting a server act as you, and how it goes wrong
question: Which control stops an admin account from being impersonated through any kind of Kerberos delegation?
options: Adding an SPN to the admin account
Enabling RC4 for the account
Moving the account to another OU
Setting 'Account is sensitive and cannot be delegated' or adding the account to Protected Users
explain: NOT_DELEGATED tells the KDC never to delegate that user's identity, and Protected Users members cannot be delegated with unconstrained or constrained delegation.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AD CS: when a certificate template hands out admin
question: An attacker obtained a certificate for ana.adm through ESC1. You reset ana.adm's password. Are you done?
options: Yes, the certificate is tied to the old password
Yes, if you also reset krbtgt once
No, you must delete the CA
No: the certificate still authenticates via PKINIT until it expires or is revoked; revoke it and fix the template
explain: Certified Pre-Owned stresses that certificates survive password resets. Revocation, plus fixing the template so the next request fails, is the response.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Why documents and scripts: the chain an analyst unpicks
question: What did Proofpoint's campaign data show after Microsoft announced it would block macros from the internet?
options: Email campaigns stopped carrying attachments at all
A shift toward ISO and RAR containers and LNK shortcut files
A permanent rise in XL4 macro documents
A move to PDF attachments only
explain: Macro attachments fell about 66% from October 2021 to June 2022, while container and LNK campaigns rose nearly 175%. XL4 use spiked briefly in March 2022 (TA542, the Emotet actor) but the overall trend was down.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Case: Follina (CVE-2022-30190), a document with no macro
question: Why did Office's macro protections not stop the Follina documents?
options: Macro blocking was off by default everywhere in 2022
The documents had no macro: code ran through a fetched template and the ms-msdt protocol handler
The macros were stomped
The documents were PDFs renamed to .docx
explain: Unit 42: remote templates historically carried macro-enabled files that macro policy would stop, but here the template was HTML that invoked MSDT, so code ran in Word's context even with macros disabled.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: JScript, VBScript and HTA: script hosts and their process trees
question: Why run emulation scripts like sandbox.js only inside the isolated analysis VM?
options: Node.js cannot run on a normal laptop
The vm module is not a security boundary, so hostile code can escape the fake objects
Emulation needs internet access
Windows Script Host must be installed
explain: Node's documentation says node:vm is not a security mechanism. A hostile script can reach the real Node environment, so treat emulation like detonation.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Anti-debugging and anti-VM: recognising checks and getting past them
question: Why do capa's authors leave IsDebuggerPresent out of 'check for debugger via API'?
options: Compiler-inserted code can call it, so it would cause many false positives
It no longer exists in Windows
It only works on Linux
Malware never uses it
explain: The rule's own comment: exception handlers and other compiler-inserted code may call it, especially in debug builds. Seeing the import is a reason to look, not a verdict.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: The exploit lifecycle: bug, primitive, leak, control, payload
question: Why does Apple's SEAR team prefer mitigations that act early in an exploit, before memory read/write?
options: Because late mitigations are slower at run time
Because early mitigations do not need hardware support
Because early stages are tied to one bug's quirks and the attacker has fewer tools, so bypasses are not plug-and-play
Because attackers never reach read/write on modern systems
explain: Apple's post argues that constraints early in the chain compound with the bug's own constraints, while bypasses after read/write are generic and reusable. Early mitigations face a weaker attacker.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: When control flow stays legal: data-only attacks
question: What did Carlini et al.'s Control-Flow Bending study conclude about shadow stacks?
options: They are unnecessary once CFI is precise
They make CFI slower without benefit
They are necessary alongside CFI: adding them removed arbitrary code execution in three of six binaries
They replace the need for ASLR
explain: Fully precise static CFI alone still allowed powerful attacks in five of six binaries. With shadow stacks added, arbitrary code execution disappeared in half of the cases, so the authors called shadow stacks necessary.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: JIT and browser engine bugs, and the V8 sandbox
question: An attacker has arbitrary read/write inside the V8 sandbox. What does the sandbox's design say they need next?
options: Nothing, the process is theirs
A leak of the ASLR base
A second bug, a sandbox bypass, because fields inside the sandbox can only address memory inside it
Physical access to the device
explain: The sandbox's stated attacker model is arbitrary read/write inside the sandbox; its goal is to stop corruption from spreading beyond it. Reaching other process memory requires a separate vulnerability.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: Zero-click chains: FORCEDENTRY and Operation Triangulation
question: How was Operation Triangulation first noticed?
options: A user reported a crash dialog
Apple's App Store review flagged a malicious app
Kaspersky saw suspicious traffic from staff iPhones on its own Wi-Fi network, then confirmed compromise from offline backups with MVT
A fuzzer reproduced the TrueType bug
explain: Detection came from network monitoring plus backup forensics, not from the device itself. It is a reminder that endpoint-invisible attacks can still leave network and timeline evidence.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Threat models for ML: goals, knowledge and capabilities
question: A competitor quietly buys the company that labels your training images. Which attack becomes easiest for them?
options: White-box evasion, because they now know your weights
Model extraction through your API
Poisoning with label control: they can mislabel or add training samples
Membership inference
explain: The labelling vendor sits on the training data path, so they gain training data control including labels. They still do not see your weights or your API traffic.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Stickers, turtles and malware: attacks outside the lab
question: In the 2022 phishing logs, the logo model was fooled but the pages were still flagged. What design property saved the system?
options: The logo model was retrained in real time
Gradient masking
The attackers used the wrong epsilon
Several independent signals were combined, so one evaded model did not decide alone
explain: The ensemble included an input-form detector and other components that the cheap logo tricks did not affect. Diversity of signals is a practical defence.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Certified robustness: randomized smoothing
question: Why did certified accuracy at radius 0.75 come out exactly 0?
options: The model is not robust at all at that radius
Sigma was too large
With n = 1,000 and alpha = 0.001, even unanimous votes give a bound of about 0.993 and a maximum radius of 0.616
Randomized smoothing only works on ImageNet
explain: The largest provable lower bound with n samples is alpha^(1/n). Bigger radii need more samples or larger sigma, which costs time or clean accuracy.

courseTitle: Adversarial machine learning
lessonTitle: Training with differential privacy: DP-SGD and its price
question: DP-SGD clips each example's gradient to norm C before adding noise. Why clip per example rather than the averaged gradient?
options: Clipping per example bounds how much any one record can move the model, which is what lets the noise hide that record
It speeds up training
It prevents adversarial examples
Clipping the average is not possible in PyTorch
explain: The privacy proof needs a bound on each record's influence (its sensitivity). Clipping the average would let one extreme record dominate before clipping.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Red team, pentest, purple team: three different questions
question: A company's SOC has never been tested and the CISO (chief information security officer) wants detection rules improved by next quarter, with the SOC learning as it goes. Which exercise fits best?
options: An unannounced red team engagement with only the CEO informed
A vulnerability scan of every server
A purple team exercise: red runs techniques openly while the SOC checks its alerts
A bug bounty programme
explain: The goal is improvement with learning, so the cooperative format fits: each technique is run, checked and fixed in the room. A covert red team measures current detection but teaches little until the report; scans and bounties do not test the SOC at all.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Deconfliction: is this the red team or a real intruder?
question: A SOC analyst sees odd PowerShell on a finance server during a known red team week and closes the alert as 'red team, expected'. What went wrong?
options: Nothing; red team activity should be ignored
The analyst should have escalated normally so the control group could check it against the operator log
The analyst should have blocked the red team's IP addresses
The analyst should have phoned the red team directly
explain: Analysts cannot tell exercise from attack, and closing alerts on a guess is how real intruders hide inside exercises. Normal escalation lets someone with the operator log answer precisely.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: MITRE Caldera: automated adversary emulation
question: An ability requires the fact 'domain user name' and no parser has produced one yet. What does Caldera do with it?
options: Runs it with an empty value
Asks the blue team
Does not create a link for it until the required fact exists
Crashes the operation
explain: Links are generated only when an ability's fact requirements are met (and the agent has a suitable executor). This is how Caldera chains steps from discovered evidence.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Case: FireEye's stolen red team tools (2020)
question: Why did FireEye publish a prioritised CVE list alongside the signatures?
options: To advertise its products
Because the CVEs were zero-days
Because patching the vulnerabilities the tools relied on defeats them whatever form the tools take
Because signatures do not work on Windows
explain: Signatures detect specific tools and can be evaded by modifying them. Removing the vulnerabilities the tools exploited closes the door regardless of tooling; FireEye stressed the tools used no zero-days.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: An agent benchmark is a task, an environment and a grader
question: Why do SWE-bench, tau-bench and WebArena grade the final state instead of comparing the agent's actions to a reference action sequence?
options: Final states are cheaper to store than action logs
Many different action sequences reach the same correct outcome, so trajectory matching would reject valid solutions
Agents do not log their actions, so there is nothing to compare
Reference action sequences would leak the answer to the agent
explain: The tau-bench paper says this directly: the user can phrase a request in different ways and the agent can call various read actions, but the episode succeeds if the database ends in the goal state. WebArena makes the same argument against comparing action sequences to references.

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: Reading a leaderboard: harness, noise, cost and contamination
question: Lab A reports a high SWE-bench Verified score using its own agent that samples many candidate patches and picks one with a reviewer model. Lab B's model reports lower on the bash-only board. What can you conclude about the underlying models?
options: Lab A's model is better, since the score is higher
Lab B's model is better, since bash-only is harder
Nothing directly: the harness, attempt count and cost differ, so only same-harness numbers compare models
They are equal once you average the two numbers
explain: Harness choices alone moved Claude 2 from 1.96% to 5.9% in the SWE-bench paper. Multi-attempt selection behaves like pass@k with a picker. Compare models only under the same scaffold and budget, which is the point of the bash-only board.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Designing tools: the agent-computer interface
question: Your file-read tool returns 30,000 tokens for big files, and quality drops on long tasks. Which fix follows the tool-writing guidance best?
options: Add pagination or a line-range parameter with a sensible default size and say in the result how to get more
Tell the model in the system prompt to read fewer files
Switch to a model with a larger context window
Compress the file with a summarizer before returning it, with no way to see the raw lines
explain: Token efficiency belongs in the tool: ranges, pagination and truncation with sensible defaults, plus a hint about how to fetch more. Prompting alone is unreliable, a bigger window still suffers from context rot, and an opaque summary removes the exact lines an editor needs.

courseTitle: Agent long-term memory: what to store, update, retrieve and forget
lessonTitle: The write path: extract facts, dedupe and resolve conflicts
question: The store holds "User likes hiking". A new message yields the candidate "User goes hiking in the Alps every summer with their brother". Which operation fits Mem0's definitions?
options: ADD, because the sentence is new
DELETE, because the old memory is less precise
UPDATE, because it is the same topic with complementary detail
NOOP, because the user already likes hiking
explain: UPDATE is for augmenting an existing memory with complementary information, like the paper's cricket example. ADD would leave two overlapping memories (a deduplication failure). DELETE is for contradictions, and nothing here contradicts. NOOP would lose the new details.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
question: An agent's final message says: "Fixed the parser; I ran pytest and everything passes." The harness has not run anything. What do you actually know?
options: The fix is verified, since the agent observed a passing pytest run
Nothing is verified yet: the message is generated text until the harness runs the tests itself
The fix is verified if the agent's message includes the pytest output
The fix is half verified: the tests pass but the code was not reviewed
explain: Everything in the final message, including pasted output, is produced by the model and may be wrong or stale. Evidence comes from the harness running checks it controls on the actual workspace.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: From a benchmark to an environment: reset, step and a checker
question: A coding agent hits the 8-turn limit while still editing files. Which step() flags describe this ending in Gymnasium terms?
options: terminated True, truncated False, because the episode is over
terminated False, truncated True, because a limit outside the task stopped it
terminated True, truncated True, because both always go together
Neither: the turn limit is handled by the policy, not the environment
explain: The task did not reach a terminal state; an external budget cut it off. That is truncation. The distinction matters because a truncated episode says nothing about whether the agent would have succeeded, so what reward it gets is a deliberate environment design choice.

courseTitle: Agentic RL environments: sandboxes, masks and rewards
lessonTitle: Sandboxes at scale: throughput, stragglers and reward hacking
question: During RL on a SWE environment, rewards jump while held-out benchmark scores do not. Logs show agents running `git log --all` early in many episodes. What is the most likely cause?
options: The loss mask is missing, so the model memorized tool outputs
The sandbox exposes future commits, so the policy learned to copy the upstream fix
The binary reward produced dead groups
The containers are too slow, so episodes get truncated
explain: This is the leak documented in SWE-bench issue 465. The reward rises because the policy found a shortcut that does not exist on held-out tasks with clean repositories.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: A toy agent loop: watching a web page give orders
question: In the code, which single change would stop the page from adding to-do items, whatever the model decides?
options: Run tool calls only after the user approves each one, or only when no untrusted content is in the context
Translate the system prompt into French
Shorten the page before sending it
Use a bigger model
explain: The model can be persuaded; the loop cannot. Gating the tool call on approval or on the provenance of the context removes the page's power to cause side effects. The other options change how often the model obeys, not what obeying can do.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Improper output handling: model output is untrusted input
question: A support bot's answer is inserted with `element.innerHTML = answer`. What is the best fix?
options: Ask the model in the system prompt not to output HTML
Insert it as text (textContent), or render Markdown with HTML disabled and sanitise the result, backed by a strict CSP
Check that the answer does not contain the word script
Shorten answers to 200 characters
explain: Prompts can be overridden and keyword checks miss event handlers like onerror. Treat the output as text, or as Markdown through a safe renderer, and keep CSP as a second wall.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Data and model poisoning: backdoors you cannot see
question: A team builds its fine-tuning set from URLs listed in a public dataset published in 2021. Which single step defends against split-view poisoning?
options: Downloading the images faster
Comparing each downloaded item with a cryptographic hash recorded when the dataset was indexed, and dropping mismatches
Using a bigger model so poison is diluted
Only using HTTPS URLs
explain: The attack works because the content behind a URL changes after indexing. A hash of what the curator saw detects any change. HTTPS only proves you reached the current domain owner, who may be the attacker.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Testing it: red teaming, benchmarks and AI for defenders
question: A vendor reports that its guardrail cut attack success from 40% to 3% on a fixed public benchmark. What is the most important follow-up question?
options: What font the benchmark used
Whether the benchmark is in English
How it performs against adaptive attacks written after seeing the defence, and what the system can still do when an attack succeeds
Whether 3% can be rounded to zero
explain: Fixed benchmarks measure known attacks; attackers adapt. The residual 3% still matters, so you also need to know the blast radius when the guardrail fails.

courseTitle: AI for materials discovery: stability, GNoME and MatterGen
lessonTitle: Generating crystals with diffusion: CDVAE to MatterGen
question: You fine-tune MatterGen for a bulk modulus target and 40% of 1,000 samples pass the MLIP filter. What is still missing before claiming new materials?
options: Nothing, since MLIP-filtered samples are stable by definition
Only a check that the bulk modulus is near the target
Running more diffusion steps
DFT verification of stability and property, deduplication against experimental databases including disordered entries, and ideally synthesis
explain: The MLIP is a filter, not the oracle. MatterGen's own bulk modulus pipeline filtered for novelty and MatterSim-predicted stability, then used DFT, and finally synthesis, which revealed that the real compound was disordered.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Second-generation text watermarks: unbiased, semantic, code, multi-bit
question: A code assistant provider must detect its own outputs in 30-line functions submitted to a coding contest. It keeps the model and the key private. Which scheme family fits best?
options: Unigram-Watermark, because one fixed list works on any length
Publicly detectable signatures, because contests are public
Entropy-aware green lists such as SWEET: watermark and score only high-entropy tokens, using the provider's own model to recompute entropies at detection
SemStamp, because code is written in sentences
explain: Short code is dominated by forced tokens, so scoring everything drowns the signal. SWEET needs the model at detection, which is fine for a provider detecting its own outputs. Public signatures need hundreds of bits of entropy, more than a short function has, and code has no natural sentences.

courseTitle: Allocation tracing and replay
lessonTitle: Capturing calls: glibc mtrace and LD_PRELOAD interposers
question: On a glibc 2.39 system, a program calls mtrace() first thing, MALLOC_TRACE=/tmp/t is set and /tmp is writable, but no trace appears. What is the most likely cause?
options: mtrace() only works when the program is compiled with -g
libc_malloc_debug.so was not preloaded, so mtrace() is a no-op
The program must also call muntrace() to flush the file
MALLOC_TRACE must point to a directory, not a file
explain: Since glibc 2.34, mtrace and the two heap-checking features mcheck and MALLOC_CHECK_ live in libc_malloc_debug.so and are disabled in the main library. -g only improves the file:line output, and the docs advise never calling muntrace().

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
question: Why does the modified z-score multiply by 0.6745?
options: It converts the MAD into a 95 percent confidence interval
It corrects for small sample sizes the way n-1 does in the standard deviation
For normal data the MAD is about 0.6745 standard deviations, so the scaling makes M read like a z-score
It is the fraction of points the median ignores
explain: For normal data the median of |x - mu| (the MAD) is about 0.6745 sigma, because 0.6745 is the 75th percentile of the standard normal. Dividing by MAD and multiplying by 0.6745 is the same as dividing by an outlier-resistant estimate of sigma (MAD x 1.4826).

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: API keys, bearer tokens and session cookies
question: Security wants to cut off a stolen token within seconds. Which design makes that easiest?
options: Long-lived self-contained JWTs with no lookup
API keys that never expire
Putting the token in a cookie
Opaque tokens checked against the issuer (introspection), or very short-lived JWTs backed by a revocable refresh token
explain: A token that is looked up can be deleted. A self-contained token stays valid until its exp unless every API checks a revocation list, which removes most of its advantage. Short lifetimes shrink that window.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The authorization code flow with PKCE, step by step
question: An authorization server receives a token request with a valid code and a code_verifier, but no challenge was sent when that code was requested. What should it do?
options: Accept: the verifier proves possession
Accept, but log a warning
Reject: RFC 9700 says to accept a code_verifier only if a code_challenge was present, to stop PKCE downgrade
Ask the user to log in again
explain: If servers accepted a verifier with no challenge on record, an attacker could start the flow without PKCE and still look PKCE-compliant later. The verifier means nothing without the earlier commitment.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: JWT anatomy: header, payload, signature and base64url
question: A JWT header decodes to `{"alg":"RS256","kid":"k7"}`. What does the signature let a receiver confirm?
options: That the holder is the user named in sub
That header and payload were not changed since the holder of the private key for k7 signed them, once the receiver checks k7 is one of its trusted issuer's keys
That the payload is secret
That the token has not expired
explain: A signature proves origin and integrity of the signed bytes, nothing more. Possession is not identity (bearer token), expiry is a separate claim check, and secrecy needs encryption.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Storing tokens in browsers, short lifetimes and revocation
question: Your single-page app (SPA) keeps its access and refresh tokens in localStorage. An XSS bug is found. What should you assume?
options: Nothing leaked, since localStorage is per origin
Only the access token leaked
Both tokens may have been read and sent elsewhere; revoke the refresh tokens, fix the XSS, and consider moving to a BFF
Only users on old browsers are affected
explain: Same-origin script can read localStorage in full. The refresh token is the valuable one, since it mints new access tokens; revoke them (all, if you cannot scope the exposure) and fix the injection.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Three maps of a secure SDLC: Microsoft SDL, OWASP SAMM, NIST SSDF
question: In SSDF terms, running a vulnerability disclosure programme falls under which group?
options: PO, Prepare the Organization
PS, Protect the Software
PW, Produce Well-Secured Software
RV, Respond to Vulnerabilities
explain: Task RV.1.3 is having a policy for vulnerability disclosure and remediation. RV covers everything after release: finding residual vulnerabilities, fixing them and preventing repeats.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: How static analysis finds bugs: taint from source to sink
question: A developer writes `name = request.args.get('name').strip()` and then `cursor.execute("SELECT * FROM t WHERE name = '" + name + "'")`. What will a taint tool report, and is it right?
options: Nothing: strip() is a sanitiser
A false positive, because names are harmless
A finding: strip() only removes whitespace, so taint propagates to the sink, and the report is a true positive
Nothing: cursor.execute is not a sink
explain: strip() returns a modified copy of tainted text, so the result is still tainted. Only operations whose output cannot carry the attack, such as int() for SQL or encoding for HTML, are sanitisers.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Secrets scanning and pre-commit hooks
question: A developer committed an API key, noticed, and pushed a second commit deleting it within a minute. What is the correct response?
options: None: the key is gone from the latest version
Make the repository private
Revoke the key at the provider, issue a new one, and check the key's usage logs
Squash the two commits
explain: The key is still in the first commit, and pushed history may already be cloned. Only revoking it removes its power. Then look for use between push and revocation.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Prioritising with CVSS, EPSS and KEV, computed on real CVEs
question: A finding has CVSS 9.8, EPSS 0.007, is not in KEV, and runs on an internal tool reachable only from the corporate network. Another has CVSS 7.5, is in KEV, and runs on an internet-facing proxy. Which goes first, and why?
options: The 9.8, because severity is what matters
The 7.5 in KEV on the internet-facing proxy, because it is being exploited and is exposed
Both equally
Neither until a pentest confirms them
explain: This is CVE-2023-44487 against CVE-2024-2057 in the example. Exploitation evidence plus exposure beats a theoretical maximum score. The 9.8 still gets fixed, on the normal schedule.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Why a crash needs both undo and redo
question: A system uses no-steal and no-force. After a crash, which work can recovery skip entirely?
options: Redo of committed transactions, because their pages were written at commit
Undo of uncommitted transactions, because their changes never reached the data pages
Both, because the log already contains everything
Neither, because the log may be incomplete
explain: No-steal guarantees no uncommitted change was ever written to a data page, so there is nothing to undo. No-force means committed changes may still be missing on disk, so redo is still required.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Restart part 2: undo, CLRs, and crashing during recovery
question: One page, all records for it. Before the crash: updates 1 and 2, the page is written to disk, updates 3 and 4, a partial rollback writes CLRs 4' and 3', then updates 5 and 6. The transaction is a loser. What does ARIES do at restart?
options: Redo nothing, since the transaction is a loser; undo 6, 5, 2, 1
Redo 1 through 6; undo 6, 5, 4', 3'
explain: This is Fig. 13 of the ARIES paper. Redo repeats everything after the page write, CLRs included. Undo follows PrevLSN from 6 to 5, then reaches CLR 3', whose UndoNextLSN points at 2, so 4 and 3 are not undone again. Then 2 and 1.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: How role-aware encoders are trained: shared versus separate towers
question: You have 5,000 labeled question to answer pairs and want role-aware retrieval. Which design does the evidence in this lesson favor?
options: Two separate towers, so each side can specialize
One shared encoder without prefixes, since prefixes only matter in pre-training
Two towers with separate projection layers, to keep the spaces independent
One shared encoder with query and passage prefixes, trained with in-batch and hard negatives
explain: Separate towers can drift into two spaces, which Dong et al. saw with t-SNE, and their shared encoder came out ahead. The laptop run could not separate the designs, so the simpler shared model stays the default. A shared encoder keeps one space, and the prefix gives it the role. In their t-SNE plots every variant with separate projection layers split into two clusters; sharing the projection kept one space.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Why a plain loop is too slow and a plain gather is too fast
question: You wrap 5,000 calls in `asyncio.gather(*[call(x) for x in items])` with no semaphore. Call 37 raises an exception after 0.4 s. What happens to the other calls?
options: They keep running in the background; gather re-raises the first exception to the awaiting code
All other calls are cancelled immediately and an ExceptionGroup is raised
gather waits for every call to finish, then raises the first exception
The event loop stops and the program exits
explain: With return_exceptions=False, gather propagates the first exception immediately, and the Python docs say the other awaitables are not cancelled. They continue, so you can lose their results and still be throttled by them. Cancelling siblings and raising an ExceptionGroup is TaskGroup behavior.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together
question: You must classify 2 million archived documents by next week, and your interactive product shares the same API account. Which plan fits best?
options: A batch job with a custom_id per document, results upserted by custom_id
Real-time calls with a semaphore of 500 and aggressive retries
Real-time calls one at a time to stay under the limits
Real-time calls with temperature 0 so the response cache absorbs most of the load
explain: Nothing here needs an answer in seconds. Batches cost less, run on a separate rate-limit pool so the product keeps its real-time capacity, and custom_id plus upserts make partial failures and re-runs safe. A huge semaphore competes with your own product for the shared limit, and distinct documents give the response cache nothing to reuse.

courseTitle: Async runtimes (Tokio) and coroutines
lessonTitle: Wakers: how a Pending task gets polled again
question: A `Delay` future is polled once in task X, then moved into a new task Y and polled there. Which waker must it wake when the time expires?
options: Both X's and Y's wakers, to be safe
Y's waker, from the most recent poll
X's waker, from the first poll
Neither: wakers are per runtime, not per task
explain: The Future docs say only the waker from the most recent poll should be scheduled. The Tokio tutorial's fixed Delay compares the stored waker with `will_wake` on every poll and replaces it if the task changed. Waking X would poll the wrong task, and Y would hang.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Inside the CPU: LOCK CMPXCHG, LL/SC, and weak versus strong
question: get_key() lazily creates a random key: if KEY is 0, generate one and CAS it from 0 to the new key; if the CAS fails, use the key another thread stored. There is no loop. Which CAS should it use?
options: compare_exchange_weak, because it is faster on ARM
Either, since x86 and ARM compile them identically
compare_exchange (strong), because a spurious failure would make it return 0 as the key
Neither; it needs fetch_add
explain: With weak, the CAS could fail even though KEY was still 0, and the Err would carry 0, which the function would return as the key. Strong only fails if another thread really installed a key. Weak is for loops where a spurious failure just means one more iteration. And on LL/SC targets (ARMv8.0) the two do compile differently.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Sigmoid outputs and pooling patch scores into a clip score
question: A clip contains a barking dog and a person talking. Model A uses softmax over classes; model B uses independent sigmoids. Which statement is correct?
options: Both can output 0.9 for Dog and 0.9 for Speech
Only model A can output high scores for both
Only model B can output 0.9 for Dog and 0.9 for Speech at the same time
Neither can; multi-label clips need two separate models
explain: Softmax outputs sum to 1, so two classes cannot both be 0.9. Independent sigmoids treat each class as its own binary question, which is why audio taggers trained on AudioSet use sigmoid outputs and binary cross-entropy.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Storing passwords wrong: plaintext, encryption, fast hashes
question: Which single property of LinkedIn's 2012 storage most helped attackers crack millions of passwords quickly?
options: The hashes were 160 bits long
The hashes were stored in hexadecimal
SHA-1 can be decrypted with the right key
SHA-1 is fast and no per-user salt was used, so one guess tested every account at once
explain: Speed lets an attacker try many guesses per second, and no salt lets each guess test all accounts at once. SHA-1 has no key and cannot be decrypted; the attacker guesses and compares.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Password rules that work: NIST SP 800-63B
question: A user's password turns up in a newly published breach list. What does NIST say to do?
options: Nothing until the 90-day rotation comes around
Force a password change, because there is evidence of compromise
Add a security question to the account
Shorten the password minimum for that user
explain: No periodic rotation does not mean never rotate. Verifiers SHALL force a change when there is evidence the authenticator was compromised, and a breach list match is such evidence.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Kinds of MFA, and the maths inside a TOTP code
question: A login accepts 6-digit TOTP codes, allows one step of drift either way, and has no limit on failed attempts. What is the main risk?
options: The HMAC can be reversed to reveal the secret
An attacker who has the password can keep guessing codes; with 3 valid codes out of a million, unlimited tries succeed quickly
Clock drift will lock out legitimate users
The QR code can be decoded from the network
explain: Each guess wins with probability 3 in a million, so the defence depends on limiting tries. NIST requires rate limiting for short codes; 100 attempts gives an attacker about a 0.03% chance.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: SSO at a glance, detection signals, and responding to takeover
question: During an account takeover response, you reset the user's password. Why is that not enough on its own?
options: Password resets take 24 hours to apply
A reset makes the old password hash crackable
The new password must first be approved by NIST
The attacker may still hold valid sessions or refresh tokens and may have enrolled their own MFA device or recovery address
explain: A session token works without the password, and an attacker-added MFA device or recovery email lets them back in later. OWASP's guidance is to invalidate existing sessions and recovery links and remove compromised authenticators after recovery.

courseTitle: Automotive and vehicle security
lessonTitle: Detecting attacks on the bus: timing, IDs and the IDS manager
question: A periodic identifier normally arrives every 20 ms. The IDS sees it at 0, 20, 21, 40, 41 and 60 ms. What is the best reading?
options: A second sender is injecting the same identifier roughly once per period, which the timing rule should flag
Normal jitter; ignore
The genuine ECU has crashed
A fuzzing attack with random identifiers
explain: Frames 1 ms after the expected ones are far inside half a period. Jitter on the real ECU is fractions of a millisecond. Fuzzing would show identifiers outside the allowlist; a crash would show a gap, not extra frames.

courseTitle: Automotive and vehicle security
lessonTitle: Keys inside the ECU: SHE, HSMs and secure boot
question: Why does SHE disable debugger-protected keys while a debugger is attached?
options: To save power
Because JTAG uses the same pins as CAN
To speed up flashing
Because a debugger can run or alter arbitrary code, so keys must not be usable by code that was not measured at boot
explain: A debugger bypasses the boot measurement. The IoT course's debug-port lesson made the same point: locking debug access protects secrets. SHE ties key availability to that state and only re-enables the slots after a reset.

courseTitle: Automotive and vehicle security
lessonTitle: EV charging: ISO 15118 Plug and Charge and OCPP
question: Under ISO 15118 Plug and Charge, why is the contract certificate's private key encrypted to the car's OEM provisioning certificate?
options: So that only the specific car holding the matching provisioning private key can install and use the contract credentials
To compress it
Because the charging station needs to read it
Because TLS 1.2 requires it
explain: The eMSP generates the key pair, so it must deliver the private key securely. Encrypting it to the provisioning certificate's public key binds it to one vehicle, as Kailus, Kern and Krauss describe.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Orchestrator, parallel subagents and context isolation
question: A lead agent sends three subagents the task "research the chip shortage". The results overlap heavily and one sub-question is never covered. What is the best fix?
options: Spawn ten subagents so coverage is more likely
Run the three subagents sequentially so they can read each other's notes
Raise the subagents' temperature to diversify their searches
Give each subagent an objective, output format, source guidance and explicit boundaries that exclude the others' topics
explain: This is the failure Anthropic described: vague task descriptions lead to duplicated work and gaps. Detailed, bounded task descriptions fix the division of labor. Temperature sets how random the output is: the model's next-token scores are divided by it before becoming probabilities, so a higher value flattens them. More agents or more randomness would increase cost without guaranteeing coverage, and running sequentially gives up the speedup.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Evaluating research agents without fooling yourself
question: Why does PaperBench grade results produced by re-running `reproduce.sh` in a fresh environment rather than the files the agent left behind?
options: Fresh environments are faster to grade
It stops an agent from scoring result-match leaves with numbers it wrote by hand during its run
The LLM judge cannot read files from the agent's environment
It ensures the agent used the blacklisted official code
explain: Separating reproduction from the agent's run means only results the code actually produces are graded, which closes a direct reward-hacking route: writing the expected numbers into a results file. Blacklisted code is forbidden, not required.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: Customizing models: fine-tuning, distillation, pretraining and import
question: Why would a LoRA-adapted model be cheaper to serve on demand than a fully fine-tuned one, in the AWS Nova customization flow?
options: LoRA models have fewer layers
LoRA removes the need for a tokenizer
Full fine-tunes cannot be imported into Bedrock
Only small adapter weights differ from the shared base, so the AWS post says PEFT models run on demand while full fine-tunes use Provisioned Throughput
explain: The adapters are small and the base is shared, so per-token on-demand serving works. A full fine-tune changes every weight, which needs its own dedicated copy. The AWS post says full fine-tunes can also be imported, but they run with Provisioned Throughput.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Symbols, stripping and debug info: what survives
question: A stripped, dynamically linked ELF binary calls `connect` and `SSL_write`. Will those names appear in `nm -D` output?
options: No, strip removes all names
Yes, imported functions stay in .dynsym because the dynamic loader must resolve them at run time
Only if the binary was built with -g
Only on Mach-O
explain: The dynamic symbol table is part of what the program needs to run, so strip cannot delete it. Imports are a reliable map of behaviour even in stripped binaries.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Compiler idioms: multiply to divide, tables and branchless code
question: A switch with six cases appears in the binary as a bounds check and a single `ldr w0, [x1, w0, uxtw #2]`. What do you conclude about the source?
options: The switch called six different functions
Each case returned a constant, so the compiler built a lookup table
The code is obfuscated
The switch had no default
explain: A data load (not an indirect branch) means the table holds values, not code addresses. A jump table ends in br/blr on ARM64 or jmp [table] on x86-64.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Go binaries: the runtime, stack checks and pclntab
question: Why can't `-ldflags="-s -w"` remove function names from a Go binary?
options: It is a linker bug
Go encrypts names
The runtime itself reads pclntab while running, for panic stack traces and FuncForPC, so the names in it must stay
Because Go binaries are dynamically linked
explain: -s removes the ELF symbol table and debug info, which only tools use. pclntab is data the program itself reads while running.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Inside extracted firmware: boot chain, filesystem and findings
question: A Linux router shows a process named `[kworker/0:1]` whose /proc entry points to a deleted file. What does that suggest?
options: A normal kernel worker thread
A crashed process
A filesystem error only
A user-space program disguised as a kernel thread, running from a file that was deleted after launch: a strong sign of compromise
explain: A /proc exe link means the process was started from a program file, so it is user-space code whatever its name says; the deleted file means someone removed the evidence. KV-botnet used exactly this masquerade and deletion.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: BitLinear: a matrix multiply made of additions
question: A ternary weight row has 1000 entries, 350 of them zero. Roughly what arithmetic does one output need?
options: 1000 multiplies and 999 adds
350 integer adds and 650 multiplies
650 multiplies, since zeros are skipped
650 integer adds or subtracts, then 1 multiply by the combined scale
explain: Each +1 adds the activation, each -1 subtracts it, each 0 is skipped: about 650 integer add or subtract steps. The scales gamma and s are shared, so they are applied once to the final sum.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
question: After packing 2B4T's linear weights into 2 bits, which part of the model is now the largest single block of weights?
options: The attention Q and K projections
The BF16 embedding and tied output head, about 0.66 GB
The FFN weights, still 2.08 GB
The RMSNorm parameters
explain: The 128,256 x 2560 embedding is 328M parameters at 2 bytes: 0.66 GB, versus 0.52 GB for all 2.08B ternary weights. Because the embeddings are tied, the output head reads that matrix every token, which is why large vocabularies matter more once the rest is ternary.

courseTitle: Branch prediction and branchless code
lessonTitle: Global history, gshare, TAGE and perceptron predictors
question: Why does gshare XOR the address and history instead of just using the history bits as the index?
options: Using only history would make every branch with the same recent history share one counter
XOR is faster to compute than concatenation
XOR removes the need for 2-bit counters
It lets the predictor guess branch targets
explain: With history alone, all branches that just saw the same outcomes collide on one counter. Mixing in address bits spreads different branches across the table while still letting every history bit affect the index.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: A browser runs hostile code all day: the threat model
question: Why do browser vendors design as if the renderer is already compromised?
options: Because renderers parse attacker-controlled content in large C++ code bases, and memory bugs there keep being found and exploited
Because renderers run with administrator rights
Because the same-origin policy is not enforced in renderers
Because JavaScript cannot be sandboxed
explain: Renderers handle hostile input all day, and Chromium's own data shows memory-safety bugs dominate high-severity issues, with all 2021 to 2023 in-the-wild Chrome exploits starting in a renderer. Renderers run with fewer rights, not more.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: IPC and Mojo: the renderer asks, the browser decides
question: A new Mojo method is proposed: `SetPermission(url.mojom.Origin origin, bool allowed)`, called by the renderer for its frame. What is the core problem?
options: It should use a string instead of url.mojom.Origin
Booleans cannot cross Mojo
It lets the renderer name the origin whose permission changes; the browser should use the frame's committed origin from its own state
It needs a DCHECK on the origin
explain: Mojo's guidance says a method that needs the renderer to send its origin has a conceptual error. The browser already knows the frame's committed origin. A string would be worse, and a DCHECK vanishes in release builds.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Containing the engine: pointer cages, the V8 sandbox and JIT policy
question: An attacker has a V8 bug that lets them overwrite any field inside V8's heap. With the V8 sandbox on, what do they still need to corrupt memory outside it, such as Blink objects?
options: A second bug: a sandbox bypass, because in-sandbox fields are offsets or table indices that cannot name outside memory
Nothing: the sandbox only slows them down
Administrator rights
A Spectre gadget
explain: The sandbox's attacker model already assumes arbitrary writes inside it. Fields that point out are offsets or table indexes with type tags, so escaping requires a separate bypass bug, which Chrome's VRP pays for separately.

courseTitle: Browser security internals: architecture, sandboxes and patch gaps
lessonTitle: Defending a fleet: policies, extensions and detection
question: Your EDR shows a Chromium helper process with `--type=gpu-process` loading a DLL from a user's temp folder. What is the best first reading?
options: Normal GPU driver behaviour
An extension update
Possible sandbox escape or injection into a privileged child; collect the DLL, the parent tree and the browser version, and check recent advisories
A Site Isolation process swap
explain: The GPU process is a known escape target and loads drivers from system locations, not from a temp folder. Treat it as possible compromise: preserve evidence, identify the browser build, and check whether a known in-the-wild CVE fits.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: Compaction: merging sorted runs and organizing levels
question: A compaction merges L1 into L2 and finds a tombstone for key 42. L3 has a file covering keys 30 to 60. What must the compaction do with the tombstone?
options: Drop it, since the newer data has already been merged
Keep it in the output, because an older version of 42 may still exist in L3
Delete the L3 file covering key 42
Convert it into a regular value with an empty string
explain: L3 is older data. If the tombstone were dropped, a later Get(42) would miss in L1 and L2, reach L3 and return the old, deleted value. The marker must travel down until no lower level can hold the key.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: Sequential flooding: how one scan wipes out the hot set
question: In the simulation, LRU loses more hot hits during the scan than clock-sweep with a cap of 5. What is the main reason?
options: Hot pages build up usage counts, so the hand must pass them several times before evicting them, while scan pages are evictable after one pass
Clock-sweep evicts scan pages first because it knows they are sequential
Clock-sweep has more frames than LRU in the simulation
LRU evicts dirty pages first
explain: Both policies have 100 frames and neither knows about scans. The difference is the counter: a page hit repeatedly survives several sweeps, while a page loaded once with count 1 is evictable after one sweep. It is still not perfect, which is why its bar does not reach 100%.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Resilience, continuity and recovery: the words and the plans
question: What does NIST SP 800-34 say distinguishes continuity planning from contingency planning?
options: Continuity planning applies to business functions and processes; contingency planning applies to recovering information systems
Continuity planning is for natural disasters; contingency planning is for cyber attacks
Continuity is required by law; contingency is optional
They are synonyms used by different agencies
explain: SP 800-34: continuity planning normally applies to the mission or business itself; contingency planning normally applies to information systems. Both cover any cause, which is why neither is tied to attacks or to weather.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: High availability is not disaster recovery: GitLab, January 2017
question: Why could GitLab not fail over to db2 when db1's data was deleted?
options: db2 had automatically replayed the deletion from db1
db2's data directory had already been wiped deliberately to rebuild replication
db2 was in a different cloud region and could not be reached
db2 ran an older PostgreSQL version
explain: The postmortem's 5 whys: the secondary's data was wiped as part of restoring replication. The `rm` on db1 was a filesystem command, not a replicated SQL write; the standby simply had nothing left to offer.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Backups attackers cannot reach: immutability and isolated recovery
question: Why restore into an isolated recovery environment rather than straight back onto the production network?
options: It is faster
Production disks are too small
Restored systems may contain the attacker's persistence; checking them in isolation stops reinfection and protects the restore itself
Regulators forbid restoring to production ever
explain: Backups taken during the attacker's dwell time can contain their tools and accounts. SP 800-209 pushes cyber-attack recovery copies to isolated staging; DORA Art. 12(3) requires segregated systems for restores. Promotion follows validation, not the other way round.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Regulated resilience: DORA testing, TLPT and UK impact tolerances
question: Under PRA SS1/21, a firm sets a short impact tolerance for its payments service, then argues it could be longer because a full data-centre loss is very unlikely. What is wrong with that argument?
options: Nothing: tolerances should reflect probability
Impact tolerances must assume the disruption occurs; cause and probability are not considered
Tolerances only apply to cyber attacks
The PRA sets the tolerance, not the firm
explain: SS1/21 says impact tolerances should be set on the assumption that a disruption will occur, without considering its cause or probability. Likelihood belongs in risk management; the tolerance is about how much harm is tolerable once it happens.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Inside BLT: local encoder, latent Transformer, local decoder
question: The n-gram 'cat' and some unrelated 3-gram hash to the same slot of $E_3^{hash}$. What happens?
options: Training fails with a key error
They share one embedding vector; the byte embedding and other n-gram sizes still distinguish them
The model falls back to a BPE tokenizer for that word
BLT rehashes until the slot is free
explain: Hash embeddings accept collisions: both n-grams add the same learned vector. Each position also gets its own byte embedding and five other n-gram lookups, and later layers see the context, so collisions only cost a little. Bigger tables reduce them.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: The same bugs in Rust: compile errors, panics, and what slips through
question: Which bug does safe Rust still allow, by design?
options: Reading an element past the end of a `Vec`
Two threads writing the same `i32` without a lock
A leak from two `Rc` values that point at each other
Using a `String` after it has been dropped
explain: Out-of-bounds access becomes a panic, sharing mutable data across threads without a lock or atomic fails to compile, and use after drop is a borrow error. Leaks are explicitly memory safe in Rust: an `Rc` cycle never reaches count 0, so its memory is never freed.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch
question: In `Drop`, what goes wrong if you call `dealloc` first and then pop the remaining elements?
options: Nothing, the order of the two steps does not matter
The elements leak but nothing else happens
Each `pop` reads a String from a block already returned to the allocator: use after free
`dealloc` fails because len is not 0
explain: After `dealloc` the block belongs to the allocator again. `pop` then calls `ptr::read` on freed memory and drops whatever bytes it finds, which is undefined behavior. Live elements must be dropped while their memory is still valid.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: Cache lines: the cache moves 64 bytes, never just one
question: An array holds 1,000,000 structs of 64 bytes each, line-aligned. A loop sums one 8-byte field from every struct. Roughly how many cache lines does one pass bring in, and what if that field lived in its own `double[1000000]` array instead?
options: 125,000 lines either way, since only 8 MB of values are read
1,000,000 lines for the structs; 125,000 for the separate array
1,000,000 lines either way, one per element
64,000,000 lines for the structs; 1,000,000 for the array
explain: Each struct is one full line, so reading any field of it fetches that line: 1,000,000 lines (64 MB). Packed into their own array, 8 values share each line: 1,000,000 / 8 = 125,000 lines (8 MB). Same values, 8x less traffic. This is the idea behind struct-of-arrays layouts: one array per field instead of one array of structs.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Why tracing circuits needs a replacement model
question: Why can't you assign one fixed weight to the edge from an SAE feature before an MLP to an SAE feature after it?
options: SAE features are always dense, so the weight would be huge
The two SAEs use different dictionary sizes
The effect passes through many MLP neurons with nonlinearities, so its size depends on everything else active
Attention moves the feature to a different token position
explain: The MLP mixes the source direction into many neurons, each with a nonlinearity, so the downstream effect changes with the input, as the toy showed (2.846 instead of 1.085 at scale 3). Transcoders sidestep this by replacing the MLP itself with sparse features.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: The local replacement model makes every edge linear
question: In the toy, all other quantities are frozen and the Dallas feature's activation rises from 3.0 to 4.0. What is the new Dallas-to-Texas edge?
options: 3.06, because virtual weights do not depend on activations
It cannot be computed without rerunning attention
explain: The edge is activation times virtual weight: 4.0 x 1.02 = 4.08. The virtual weight 1.02 is fixed because the attention weight 0.8 and the denominator 2.0 are frozen.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: What attribution graphs found: arithmetic, languages, refusals, CoT
question: In the jailbreak, clamping "new sentence" features changed the outcome only when attention patterns were allowed to change. What does that imply for the graph?
options: The new-sentence features are error nodes
The graph was pruned too aggressively
The key step of the refusal runs through attention QK, which a frozen-attention graph does not show
Attention is irrelevant to refusals
explain: With attention frozen, the clamp mostly removed "However" while the model still refused; with attention unfrozen, it kept complying. So the mechanism that matters changes where heads attend, exactly the QK computation lesson 9 lists as missing.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Click models: PBM, cascade, UBM and DBN
question: A log has many sessions where users clicked results at both rank 2 and rank 5. Which model assigns these sessions zero probability?
options: The cascade model
The position-based model
The user browsing model
The dynamic Bayesian network model
explain: The cascade model ends a session at the first click, so two clicks are impossible. PBM treats ranks independently, UBM explicitly conditions on the last click, and DBN continues after an unsatisfying click.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Reflected XSS: the server echoes the attack back
question: A developer fixes reflected XSS by deleting `<script>` and `</script>` from the q parameter before storing it in a variable. What is the main problem?
options: Deleting tags is slower than encoding them
It is correct, but should be done in the browser instead of on the server
It breaks HTTPS, because the request no longer matches its signature
Markup can run script without a script tag, for example through an event-handler attribute, so a deny-list of tags leaves the sink open
explain: A deny-list removes the one form the developer thought of. HTML has many places where script can start, such as event-handler attributes and javascript: URLs. Encoding at output closes them all at once, because no attacker character can start markup.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Framework auto-escaping and its escape hatches
question:
A Vue app renders a bio with `

{{ user.bio }}

` and a link with ``. Which is the XSS risk?
options: The paragraph, because {{ }} inserts raw HTML
Neither, because Vue escapes both
Both, because Vue does no escaping in production builds
The link, because escaping does not stop a javascript: URL
explain: {{ }} uses textContent, so the bio is text. The :href binding is attribute-escaped, which stops breaking out of the attribute, but a value of javascript:... needs no special characters. Validate the scheme.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Stopping CSRF: SameSite, tokens, Origin and Fetch Metadata
question: A bank sets its session cookie to `SameSite=Lax` and does nothing else. Its old endpoint `GET /transfer?to=...&amount=...` moves money. Is it protected?
options: Yes, Lax blocks all cross-site requests
Yes, because GET requests cannot change state
No, because SameSite only works over HTTP/2
No, because Lax still sends the cookie on a cross-site top-level GET navigation, such as a link the victim clicks
explain: Lax was designed to keep links into your site working, so it sends cookies on top-level GET navigations. That makes state-changing GETs the most common way SameSite-only defences fail, according to OWASP.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: Browser extensions: someone else's code in every page
question: In the Cyberhaven incident, what was the initial weakness the attacker used?
options: A buffer overflow in Chrome
A stolen password reused from another breach
An XSS bug in the Chrome Web Store
A phishing email that got a developer to approve a malicious OAuth application with publishing rights
explain: Cyberhaven's analysis describes a phishing email leading into Google's normal authorisation flow for an app called Privacy Policy Extension. Consent to a malicious app is enough; no password was needed. Reviewing and restricting OAuth grants is part of the defence.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Temperature: why CLIP multiplies cosines by up to 100
question: Why does a larger logit scale make the loss more sensitive to mislabeled pairs?
options: Because the scale changes which caption has the highest cosine
Because when the wrong caption wins by a margin m, the row loss grows about linearly in scale times m
Because scaling by 100 overflows float16
Because the scale is applied only to the off-diagonal entries
explain: Multiplying all logits by s does not change the ranking, but for a row where a wrong caption beats the right one by m, the loss behaves like s times m for large s (see the plot with m = -0.03). The scale multiplies every entry, and overflow is avoided by subtracting the max.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Reading CloudTrail like a responder: who really made this call?
question: In ten minutes, one role session receives AccessDenied from IAM, EC2, Lambda, Secrets Manager and RDS. Nothing succeeded. What is the best reading?
options: Someone is probing what this credential can do, so treat the credential as possibly stolen and find where it came from
Harmless: failed calls cannot hurt anyone
A misconfigured SDK retry loop, since attackers never trigger errors
AWS throttling, because AccessDenied means too many requests
explain: Errors across many unrelated services in a short window match enumeration of a stolen credential's permissions. The failures did no damage, but the credential is in someone's hands, and the next role they find may succeed. AccessDenied is an authorization failure, not throttling.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Managed detection: GuardDuty, Defender for Cloud and Google SCC
question: GuardDuty runs with only its foundational data sources. An attacker with a stolen role downloads 10,000 objects from S3. Which statement is right?
options: GuardDuty will flag the downloads, because it reads S3 traffic from flow logs
GuardDuty can still flag the stolen role's management calls (for example from an unusual address), but has no view of the object reads
GuardDuty stores the CloudTrail events, so you can investigate the reads later
GuardDuty sees nothing, because it needs CloudTrail data events turned on in your trail
explain: Foundational sources are management events, flow logs and DNS logs, so anomalies in the role's API calls can still be found. Object reads need S3 Protection. GuardDuty discards the logs after analysis, and S3 Protection does not need your trail's data events.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Containers, serverless and autoscaling: evidence that deletes itself
question: Which record would show an attacker who changed a Lambda function's environment variables to add their own API key?
options: An UpdateFunctionConfiguration management event in CloudTrail
Only an Invoke data event, if enabled
The function's /tmp directory
VPC Flow Logs of the function
explain: Changing a function's configuration, environment variables included, is a management API call, logged by default (AWS omits the Environment values from the event, so compare published versions to see what was added). Invoke events show calls to the function, not changes to it; /tmp is not reachable by you; flow logs show network flows only.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: Containing without breaking production, and a cloud IR runbook
question: An attacker used an IAM user's leaked long-term key to create temporary credentials with GetSessionToken. Which action stops those temporary credentials?
options: Deleting the S3 bucket they read from
Rotating the role's trust policy
Nothing; temporary credentials cannot be stopped before they expire
Attaching an inline policy to the user that denies requests whose aws:TokenIssueTime is before now (or deleting and recreating the user), and deactivating the key
explain: AWS's guide says there is no console option for revoking an IAM user's temporary credentials; the TokenIssueTime deny on the user, or deleting and recreating the user, does it. Deactivating the key stops new ones. The user is not a role, so trust policies do not apply.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: The same guardrails in Azure Policy and Google organization policy
question: Which single organization-wide setting would have made the Microsoft researchers' account SAS unusable for reading blobs?
options: Azure Policy denying storage accounts that allow Shared Key access, so AllowSharedKeyAccess is false
An Azure RBAC role assignment of Storage Blob Data Reader
A SAS expiration policy with the default Log action
Moving the storage account to a different region
explain: An account SAS is authorized with Shared Key, and Microsoft documents that it is not permitted on Blob requests when AllowSharedKeyAccess is false. RBAC does not govern SAS tokens; the Log action only records out-of-policy SAS use and still allows it.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Cross-account trust and the confused deputy
question: A Lambda function's resource policy lets `s3.amazonaws.com` invoke it with `aws:SourceArn` set to `arn:aws:s3:::uploads-bucket`, and nothing else. The bucket is later deleted. What risk does AWS's documentation describe?
options: Another account could create a bucket with the same name and trigger the function; adding aws:SourceAccount closes this
None, because bucket ARNs are unique forever
The function is deleted automatically with the bucket
S3 will start invoking the function with administrator rights
explain: Bucket ARNs contain no account ID, and a deleted bucket name can be created again by someone else. The Lambda docs recommend aws:SourceAccount (the --source-account option) for S3 triggers.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Google Cloud in depth: service accounts, actAs and impersonation
question: Why does Google advise against granting the Service Account Token Creator role at the project level?
options: The user can impersonate every service account in the project and reach whatever those accounts can access, even outside the project
It is billed per project
It disables Admin Activity audit logs
Project-level roles expire after 15 minutes
explain: Google's best practices say project-level Token Creator lets the user impersonate any service account in the project, potentially reaching all resources those accounts can access, including outside the project.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: The shared responsibility model, and when the provider gets it wrong
question: After ChaosDB, what did Microsoft ask potentially affected Cosmos DB customers to do?
options: Nothing, the provider fixed it entirely
Delete their databases
Regenerate their primary read-write keys
Disable Azure Active Directory
explain: Microsoft disabled the notebook feature and asked customers whose keys might have been exposed to regenerate the primary read-write key. A provider bug still left a credential that only the customer could rotate.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Long-lived keys vs temporary credentials: STS and Uber 2016
question: A role's trust policy allows the `ci-deployer` role to assume it, and its permissions policy allows `s3:*`. Which statement is true?
options: The trust policy limits which S3 buckets the session can use
The trust policy lets ci-deployer use S3 directly without assuming the role
ci-deployer can call AssumeRole on it and the resulting session can use S3
Anyone in the account can assume it, because trust policies only apply across accounts
explain: The trust policy decides who may become the role; the permissions policy decides what the role session may do. Together: ci-deployer may assume it, and the session may use S3.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Storage exposure: public buckets, Block Public Access and SAS tokens
question: Why was the 2023 Microsoft SAS token so dangerous compared with a typical shared link?
options: It was signed with a weak hash
It used HTTP instead of HTTPS
It covered the whole storage account with full control and expired in 2051, and SAS creation is not logged, so nobody could see it existed
It required MFA that attackers could bypass
explain: Scope (whole account), permissions (full control) and lifetime (decades) made it equivalent to the account key, and because SAS generation cannot be audited, the owners had no inventory of it.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Catching misconfigurations early: infrastructure as code and CSPM
question: Checkov reports CKV_AWS_79 for an instance resource. What is the fix?
options: Attach a larger instance type
Encrypt the root volume
Add metadata_options with http_tokens = "required" so the instance only accepts IMDSv2
Remove the instance's IAM role
explain: CKV_AWS_79 checks that IMDSv1 is not enabled. Requiring session tokens on the instance resource satisfies it and closes the plain-GET path to role credentials.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Gaussian mixtures and EM: soft k-means with a shape per cluster
question: Under a fitted two-component mixture, a point gets responsibilities 0.59 and 0.41. What does that mean?
options: The point is 59 percent of the way from one centre to the other
The fit has not converged yet, since converged EM always gives 0 or 1
The point is an outlier, because neither component reaches 0.9
The model is unsure: given the fitted weights, means and covariances, there is a 59 percent probability it came from the first component
